stimulus.text:
Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776:

“I long to hear that you have declared an independency. I desire you would remember the ladies and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the husbands. Remember, all men would be tyrants if they could. If particular care and attention is not paid to the ladies, we are determined to foment a rebellion, and will not hold ourselves bound by any laws in which we have no voice or representation.”
stimulus.source_note: Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776. Founders Online, National Archives. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776. Public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals
The American Revolution and Its Aftermath

primary_sources: Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776

stem: The letter best illustrates which broader development of the revolutionary era?

options.text: Revolutionary ideas about tyranny and representation were taken up by women.
The Continental Congress granted women equal political rights in 1776.
options.misconception: Background: Congress granted women no political rights in 1776; Adams was asking for change that did not come.

options.text: Most women in 1776 opposed independence from Britain.
options.misconception: The letter shows Adams eager for independence, and it says nothing about most women opposing it.

options.text: Marriage law was the only subject of debate in the new republic.
options.misconception: Marriage law was one debate among many, including slavery, religion, and the structure of government.

rationales.A: Adams uses the language of tyranny and representation, the Revolution’s own ideas, to challenge husbands’ power.
rationales.B: The letter is a request for change, not proof that Congress granted women rights.
rationales.C: Adams longs to hear independence declared, which points the other way.
rationales.D: The letter is about one debate; it does not claim marriage law was the only debate.
rationales.general:
1. The letter warns that all men would be tyrants if they could.
2. It says women will not be bound by laws in which they have no voice or representation.
3. Background: tyranny and representation were the Revolution’s central ideas, aimed first at the king.
4. So the letter shows those ideas being taken up by women to challenge their own position.
Remember: ideas from a revolution often get applied to groups the revolution first left out.
